fake_negative_hypotheses: The precise spatiotemporal modulation of TGF-β and BMP signaling pathways will be achieved through a combination of gradient-based delivery systems and temporally controlled exposure protocols, optimized to specific concentrations (e.g., TGF-β at 10-100 ng/mL and BMP-2 at 50-200 ng/mL) administered at defined intervals (e.g., continuous for 72 hours followed by pulsed exposure for key differentiation windows), to enhance the differentiation of pluripotent stem cells into osteoblasts (assessed via alkaline phosphatase activity and mineralization assays) and chondrocytes (validated by collagen type II expression). This approach aims to uncover novel pathways of signaling integration and its implications for treating skeletal disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta and degenerative joint diseases.

The integration of a dynamic microfluidic platform that modulates spatiotemporal gradients of TGF-β (0–100 ng/mL) and BMP (0–200 ng/mL) signaling, alongside specific mechanical and biochemical cues within a three-dimensional (3D) biomimetic hydrogel scaffold, will enhance the differentiation of pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) into osteoblasts and chondrocytes, ultimately improving skeletal development outcomes and providing a novel therapeutic strategy for osteogenesis imperfecta and degenerative joint diseases.

The co-delivery of bioengineered exosomes derived from mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) preconditioned with specified optimal concentrations of TGF-β1 (10 ng/mL) and BMP-2 (50 ng/mL) will synergistically enhance the regenerative capacity of aging cartilage by promoting chondrocyte differentiation and cartilage matrix synthesis. This will be achieved through the targeted release of a defined set of growth factors and regulatory proteins, including IL-10 and VEGF, alongside the transcription factors SOX9 and RUNX2. The use of a biodegradable scaffold composed of collagen-based materials, specifically designed to replicate the mechanical and biochemical properties of the aging cartilage microenvironment, will facilitate optimal cellular interactions and signaling pathways, thereby maximizing the regenerative effects.

Variants in the BMP5 gene, specifically missense mutations impacting protein stability and receptor binding, disrupt the canonical BMP signaling pathway, leading to impaired osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation. This dysregulation contributes to skeletal dysostosis and associated phenotypes, including atrioventricular septal defect, as evidenced by altered gene expression and differentiation profiles in patient-derived iPSCs subjected to CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing.

Variations in the BMP5 gene, particularly the c.1136delC and c.960C>T mutations, lead to disruptions in the BMP signaling cascade, resulting in altered expression patterns of critical osteogenic and chondrogenic transcription factors such as Runx2, Osx, and Sox9. This disruption mediates the pathophysiological processes underlying skeletal dysostosis and associated developmental anomalies, including cardiac defects. By employing an integrated CRISPR-Cas9 and CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) technique with optimized viral vector delivery into primary osteoblasts and chondrocytes, this study aims to quantitatively assess the differential roles of BMP5 in regulating transcription factor expression. Concurrently, we will evaluate how modulating downstream targets will influence cellular differentiation and other phenotypic outcomes. This comprehensive approach will elucidate the mechanistic pathways linking BMP5 variants to skeletal formation and enable the identification of novel therapeutic targets for bone and cartilage disorders, ultimately informing future interventions.
gold_hypothesis: A detailed understanding of TGF-β and BMP signaling pathways, including their regulatory mechanisms and interactions with other signaling pathways, can elucidate their roles in skeletal development and disease, leading to novel therapeutic strategies for bone and cartilage disorders by precisely targeting these pathways.
model_negative_hypotheses: A novel research hypothesis is that by leveraging the cross-talk mechanisms between BMP and TGF-β signaling pathways, specifically through the strategic manipulation of Wnt pathway components, we can enhance the differentiation and function of osteoblasts and chondrocytes. This can be achieved by using IWP2 at a concentration of 1 μM administered every 24 hours for 7 days, combined with CRISPR/Cas9 to upregulate β-catenin via a guide RNA sequence targeting exon 3 of the β-catenin gene, with an expected editing efficiency of 80% in primary osteoblast and chondrocyte cultures. The differentiation and function of osteoblasts and chondrocytes will be monitored using Alizarin Red staining at day 7 post-treatment and gene expression analysis for markers such as RUNX2 and COL2A1 using qPCR with primers specific to these genes.

BMP receptor-specific agonists and antagonists can be rationally designed using advanced computational tools (e.g., AutoDock Vina for docking simulations, GROMACS for molecular dynamics) and validated through biochemical and cell-based assays to selectively modulate the signaling pathways of Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β) and Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (BMPs) for regulating osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation, skeletal development, and homeostasis. Additionally, the activation of TGF-β and BMP signaling pathways in osteoblasts and chondrocytes can be precisely controlled by mechanical forces exerted through integrin binding (specifically αvβ6 for TGF-β and αvβ3 for BMPs) and the unfastening of the prodomain "straitjacket" through the application of tensile forces with a magnitude of 10 N for a duration of 30 seconds. These dual approaches will provide a comprehensive therapeutic strategy for treating bone and cartilage disorders, with potential applications in other areas such as wound healing and tissue regeneration.

By leveraging the structural insights of BMP9 prodomains and Noggin, we can design and implement a novel bi-specific antibody approach that simultaneously binds to the prodomain of BMP9 and Noggin. Specifically, the first arm of the antibody will target the prodomain of BMP9 to stabilize its active form and promote receptor binding, while the second arm will target Noggin to either enhance or inhibit BMP signaling. Validation will be conducted using Western blotting to confirm antibody binding, ELISA to measure BMP signaling modulation, and cell differentiation assays to evaluate changes in osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation. This bi-specific antibody approach is novel because it specifically targets the prodomain of BMP9 and Noggin, filling a gap in current BMP signaling regulation techniques that often lack the precision and specificity offered by this method. This approach offers a more precise and controlled method for regulating osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation, skeletal development, and homeostasis, thus providing a novel therapeutic avenue for treating bone and cartilage disorders and influencing future drug design strategies in regenerative medicine.

We hypothesize that a multi-pronged therapeutic strategy combining (1) temporally and spatially controlled release of a conformationally stabilized, photo-caged BMP-4 prodomain-derived peptide, (2) highly selective inhibition of Smurf1 E3 ubiquitin ligase activity via optimized small molecules, and (3) precisely modulated cyclic tensile force stimulation, mimicking the spatiotemporal dynamics of αvβ3 integrin engagement with latent TGF-β1, will synergistically drive robust, localized, and temporally regulated osteoblast differentiation in MSCs, while concurrently suppressing chondrogenesis, leading to enhanced bone regeneration and reduced cartilage degeneration in a pre-clinical osteoarthritis model. This will be achieved through:
1.  Spatially and Temporally Controlled BMP-4 Prodomain-Derived Peptide Release:
       Peptide Design: We will design a photo-cleavable, caged BMP-4 prodomain-derived peptide based on the sequence encompassing residues 68-78 of the prodomain (sequence: [Provide the actual sequence]). The peptide will incorporate N-methylated L-amino acids at positions 70 and 74 to enhance proteolytic stability and trans-amide bond formation; a D-beta-amino acid at position 72 and an L-beta-amino acid at position 76 to induce and lock a stable alpha-helical conformation that mimics the native conformation of the prodomain upon ligand binding; a PEGylated (4-arm branched PEG, 5kDa, linked via a maleimide group) lysine residue at position 78 (the C-terminal) to enhance cellular permeability and reduce non-specific binding, a 2-Nitrobenzyl ether-based photocleavable linker, and a Cy5 fluorescent tag at the N-terminal for tracking. The peptide will be synthesized using Fmoc solid-phase peptide synthesis and purified via HPLC to >95% purity. The peptide's binding affinity to BMP-4 ligand will be quantified using MST, determining the Kd value. Confocal microscopy will be used to assess cellular uptake and intracellular distribution of the Cy5-labeled peptide.
       Hydrogel Encapsulation: The peptide will be encapsulated within a biocompatible, biodegradable methacrylated gelatin (GelMA) hydrogel matrix with a pore size of 50-100 μm, synthesized via UV-initiated free radical polymerization using 0.5% (w/v) Irgacure 2959 photoinitiator, and crosslinked with 5mM cystamine to achieve a degradation rate of 2-3 days in vitro. The hydrogel will be deposited to a specific area of the MSCs in vitro, and will be locally injected into the injured cartilage of the mouse model in vivo. A 405nm light exposure will be applied in a pulsatile manner at 0, 24, and 48 hours to uncage the peptide. Release kinetics of the peptide will be monitored using confocal microscopy by quantifying the Cy5 signal over time and quantified through ImageJ.
2.  Targeted Smurf1 Inhibition using Optimized Small Molecules:
       Virtual Screening and Compound Selection: We will utilize a structure-based virtual screening approach targeting the HECT domain of Smurf1 using a filtered library of 100,000 molecules from the Enamine REAL library. The filters will prioritize molecules with molecular weight ranging from 350-500 Da, a clogP value between -1 and 5, fewer than 10 hydrogen bond acceptors, less than 5 hydrogen bond donors, less than 10 rotatable bonds, and no reactive groups. Screening criteria will include an energy-minimized structure docking score of -8 kcal/mol or lower against the binding pocket of the Smurf1 HECT domain, using Glide software (Schrodinger). The selected top 100 molecules will be purchased and experimentally screened.
      High-Throughput Screening: A cell-based high-throughput screen will be performed using a luciferase-based autoubiquitination assay of Smurf1 as a readout. IC50 values will be determined for each compound using purified Smurf1 in enzymatic assays and by assessing the ubiquitination level of Smad1/5/8 in MSCs using immunoprecipitation and Western blot, with secondary confirmation using mass spectrometry to measure Smad ubiquitination level. Selectivity will be verified by evaluating off-target ubiquitination activity using proteomic analysis of cell lysates. The lead compound will be further optimized through chemical synthesis to enhance the potency and improve drug-likeness properties via medicinal chemistry approaches to synthesize analogs with improved bioavailability and metabolic stability.
3.  Cyclic Tensile Force Application via Microfluidic Device:
       Device Fabrication: A custom-fabricated microfluidic device will be used, incorporating fibronectin-coated polyacrylamide hydrogels. The hydrogels will be composed of 10% (w/v) acrylamide and 0.3% (w/v) bis-acrylamide. The hydrogels will be covalently conjugated with fibronectin (10 μg/mL) via a heterobifunctional cross-linker, sulfo-SANPAH. The device will be made using a PDMS cast, and be assembled on a glass slide, with an inlet and an outlet for the media. A micro-scale hydraulic actuator coupled with a force sensor will apply cyclic tensile force of 25 kPa with a frequency of 1 Hz. The tensile force will be applied along the length of the cell for 24 hours in a cyclic manner, in vitro. The force will be applied on the cell through controlled displacement of the hydrogel via the hydraulic actuator.
       Mechanical Stimulation Control and Validation: The displacement of the hydrogel will be precisely controlled by a feedback loop controlling the hydraulic actuator. The force will be calibrated using a force sensor integrated within the device. The force transmission on the cell will be validated using traction force microscopy. The expression and activation of the integrin will be measured using FACS and immunofluorescence. The effect of the tensile force on latent TGF-β1 activation will be evaluated by immunofluorescence staining using antibodies specific for the active form of TGF-β1, and quantified by western blot for the p-SMAD2/3. To verify the specificity of integrin activation of the mechanical force, the RGD sequence on the prodomain will be blocked using a specific anti-RGD antibody (10ug/mL). This will verify the reduction of the active TGF-β1 level and downstream signaling.
4.  Combined Stimulation of MSCs In Vitro:
     Primary mouse MSCs will be pre-treated with the photo-caged BMP-4 peptide, followed by pulsed light exposure at 0, 24 and 48 hours. Separately, MSCs will be treated with varying concentrations of the selected Smurf1 inhibitor (0.1-10µM, based on the IC50 determined) and cyclic tensile force (25kPa, 1Hz), both individually and in combinations.
       Signaling Pathway Analysis: Phosphorylation levels of SMAD1/5/9, SMAD2/3, ERK, p38, and Akt will be measured using Western blotting. Detailed proteomic analysis with phosphoproteomics using mass spectrometry will be performed, focusing on early time points (0, 15, 30, 60 min) after each stimulation to identify differential temporal activation patterns.
       Gene and Protein Expression Analysis: Osteoblast marker genes (RUNX2, OCN, ALPL, COL1A1) and chondrocyte marker genes (SOX9, COL2A1, ACAN) will be analyzed using qPCR and confirmed by immunofluorescence staining. Protein levels will be evaluated by Western blotting and lineage-specific markers such as CD105, osteopontin, and collagen X will be measured.
       Cell Differentiation Assessment: Osteoblast differentiation will be quantified using alkaline phosphatase activity, Alizarin Red staining, and Von Kossa staining. Chondrocyte differentiation will be quantified using glycosaminoglycan production assays, collagen II deposition (immunofluorescence), and expression of collagen X (qPCR and immunofluorescence).
       Single-Cell RNA-Sequencing: Single-cell RNA-seq will be used to map the heterogeneity of the MSC population and identify the effects of the combined treatment on cell fate trajectories, focusing on the synergistic interactions between the three interventions. A pseudo-time analysis will identify cells following an osteogenic vs. chondrogenic trajectory.
       Synergy Analysis: Synergy between the three interventions will be quantitatively assessed using the Excess over Bliss (EOB) model, calculating synergy scores for all combinations. A positive EOB score above 15% will be considered significant.
5.  In Vivo Efficacy and Safety Assessment:
       Animal Model: We will use an 8-week-old female C57BL/6 mouse model of osteoarthritis induced by intra-articular injection of monosodium iodoacetate (MIA, 1mg/5ul in saline). The MIA model is chosen because it rapidly induces OA-like changes, including cartilage degradation and subchondral bone changes in a relatively short time frame, with minimal inflammation. The photo-caged BMP-4 peptide (10 mg/kg, based on pilot in vivo study), Smurf1 inhibitor (5 mg/kg, based on pilot in vivo study) and mechanical stimulation (25kPa, 1Hz, for 24hrs) will be locally injected/applied to the target area (knee joint) via intra-articular injection, with the mechanical stimulation provided by a custom-made, wearable vibration device (2cm x 2cm x 1 cm) powered by a 3V battery and controlled by a micro-controller. The device is composed of a vibration motor that will transfer mechanical force to the injection site through a custom made, 3D printed, soft polymeric interface. The treatment will be performed once every other day for 4 weeks.
       Outcome Assessment: Changes in bone and cartilage will be assessed using micro-CT, histological analyses with Safranin-O staining for cartilage and Masson's Trichrome staining for bone, and biomechanical testing, assessing joint stiffness and load-bearing capacity using a four-point bending test.
       Safety Monitoring: Safety will be evaluated by monitoring for ectopic ossification, inflammation, pain behavior (paw withdrawal test), and any other adverse effects. Blood samples will be collected to perform a complete blood count (CBC) test, comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), liver function test (LFT), and inflammatory cytokines levels at different time points after the injection and at the end of the treatment.
      Statistical Analysis: The sample size will be set at 6 mice per group to achieve a statistical power of 0.8, and two-way ANOVA will be performed to evaluate the differences between the groups. Post-hoc multiple comparisons will be performed using Tukey's HSD test if ANOVA shows significant results.
6.  Mechanism Validation:
       Smurf1 Substrate Identification: Immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry (IP-MS) will be used to identify specific Smurf1 substrates in MSCs, focusing on the ubiquitination levels of known substrates such as Smad1/5/8 and novel substrates identified after the treatment.
       Force-Mediated TGF-β1 Activation Mechanism: The dynamic conformational change of the TGF-β1 prodomain under mechanical stress, and its interaction with αvβ3 integrins, will be evaluated using FRET (Förster resonance energy transfer) with the following approach: MSCs will be transfected with a TGF-β1 prodomain tagged with mTurquoise2 at the N-terminus, and with a monomeric αvβ3 integrin tagged with mVenus at the C-terminus of the β3 subunit. A change in the fluorescence of the acceptor and the donor will indicate the interaction of the prodomain with the integrin, upon application of the mechanical stress. This will be further analyzed by time-lapse confocal microscopy during the cyclic tensile force application.

Aberrant Glycosylation at these Sites, or Disruption of Endoglin Binding, Will Impair Chondrocyte Differentiation and Contribute to Skeletal Dysplasia.

The specific interaction between Smad-dependent BMP signaling and the PI3K/Akt pathway, mediated by Akt1 andAkt2, plays a crucial role in regulating osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation during distinct developmental stages, by crosstalk with the MAPK/ERK pathway through p38 MAPK and ERK1/2, leading to the activation of downstream targets such as Runx2, Sox9, and ACVR1B, which are essential for normal skeletal development. Disrupting this crosstalk specifically leads to abnormal skeletal development, increased susceptibility to bone and cartilage disorders, and identifies novel therapeutic targets for treating these conditions.

The mechanical force-dependent activation of latent TGF-β and BMPs through integrin binding and conformational changes in the prodomain can be precisely modulated using a multi-faceted approach that integrates microfluidic devices, magnetic tweezers, and designer peptides/small molecules. This combined strategy will target specific integrin subtypes (e.g., αvβ3, αvβ6, αvβ8) and key residues or domains within the prodomain to either enhance or inhibit TGF-β/BMP signaling pathways. By stabilizing or destabilizing the 'straitjacket' mechanism and modulating integrin interactions, this approach aims to precisely control osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation, promoting skeletal development and homeostasis. The research will provide novel therapeutic strategies for bone and cartilage disorders.

We hypothesize that targeted disruption of the disulfide bond within the "straitjacket" region of the TGF-β prodomain, using a reducing agent (DTT) delivered via a micro-encapsulated system, will facilitate the release of active TGF-β1 independent of mechanical force, leading to a controlled and localized promotion of osteoblast differentiation in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). Specifically, the microcapsules will be fabricated using poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) with a size range of 1-5 μm using a double emulsion method. These microcapsules will be coated with an Eudragit L100-55 pH-sensitive polymer that will swell and degrade at a pH of 7.6, leading to the release of the encapsulated DTT. The encapsulated reducing agent will consist of dithiothreitol (DTT) at a concentration of 5 mM, which has been determined through a dose-response curve to be sufficient in disrupting the disulfide bond while minimizing cell toxicity. The MSCs will be cultured with the micro-encapsulated DTT for 48 hours. Osteoblast differentiation will be quantified by measuring the expression levels of osteocalcin, a late marker of osteoblast differentiation, using qRT-PCR, at 24h, 48h, and 72h post-treatment, with a threshold of a 10-fold increase relative to the control group, which is based on literature for a positive osteoblast differentiation result. Furthermore, the release of active TGF-β1 will be assessed via ELISA using antibodies specific to the active form of TGF-β1, and levels of phosphorylated SMAD2/3 will be measured using Western blotting, all at 24h, 48h and 72h post treatment. Control groups will include MSCs treated with microcapsules containing PBS, MSCs exposed to micro-encapsulated DTT that has been chemically treated with iodoacetamide to neutralize the reducing agent activity, and MSCs treated with free DTT (5mM) to evaluate potential DTT-induced cytotoxicity, which will be measured by MTS assay at 24h, 48h, and 72h post treatment. The possibility of off-target effects will be evaluated by measuring changes in the expression of key genes in other signaling pathways, including Wnt, Notch, and MAPK pathways, and by performing a whole-cell protein assay (LC-MS/MS based proteomic analysis) to identify changes in other disulfide bonds. We hypothesize that the PLGA microcapsules will be internalized by MSCs via an endocytosis mechanism, which will be assessed using confocal microscopy imaging of fluorescently labeled microcapsules, and TEM imaging to visualize the intracellular location of the microcapsules. By leveraging the slightly alkaline microenvironment prevalent in early stages of bone formation, the release of the reducing agent is maximized in the context of promoting MSC differentiation towards osteoblasts. This approach offers precise chemical control over the TGF-β pathway and has the potential to be translated into diverse tissue engineering applications, such as promoting bone regeneration in vivo, with improved spatio-temporal control and reduced reliance on mechanical stimulation. The proposed method will be advantageous in localized and controlled TGF-β delivery for bone repair with improved and tunable control than previous mechanical and thermal strategies, overcoming the issue of wide stimulation.

The force-dependent activation mechanism of latent TGF-β, mediated by α<sub>v</sub>β integrin binding (specifically α<sub>v</sub>β<sub>3</sub> and α<sub>v</sub>β<sub>5</sub>) and mechanical tension (e.g., 10% cyclic tensile strain at 1 Hz for 24 hours), plays a critical role in regulating osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation during skeletal development and homeostasis. This mechanobiological activation mechanism is distinct from traditional biochemical pathways, such as BMP signaling, and is uniquely suited to skeletal tissues due to their dynamic mechanical loading environment. By leveraging this mechanism, it is possible to develop targeted therapies, such as biomaterials or mechanical devices, that modulate TGF-β activation with high specificity and reduced side effects. These therapies could be tested in vitro using osteoblast and chondrocyte cultures subjected to controlled mechanical forces in bioreactor systems, with TGF-β activation and downstream signaling measured via immunofluorescence, Western blot, and gene expression analysis. Control experiments will rule out alternative pathways, such as cross-talk with other integrins or mechanosensors, ensuring the validity of the approach. This research not only advances the treatment of bone and cartilage disorders like osteoporosis and osteoarthritis but also provides a model for studying force-dependent signaling in other mechanosensitive tissues.

The integration of atomic-level structural insights into BMP ligand-receptor interactions—specifically targeting the unique binding pockets formed by residues such as Arg74 and Asp80 in the BMP9 prodomain-ligand interface and the conformational dynamics of the BMPR-II and ALK2 receptor heterocomplexes—with the modulation of BMP-TGF-β signaling cross-talk, mediated by shared transcriptional co-regulators (e.g., Ski and SnoN) and ubiquitin ligase activity (e.g., Smurf1), offers a novel, dual-targeted therapeutic strategy for bone and cartilage disorders. By designing small-molecule inhibitors that mimic the natural ligand-binding motifs and monoclonal antibodies targeting epitopes on BMPR-II and ALK2, we propose to selectively modulate BMP signaling while simultaneously fine-tuning TGF-β cross-talk. This approach will be validated through computational docking (using Rosetta and AutoDock Vina with AMBER force fields), molecular dynamics simulations (to assess conformational stability and binding affinities), in vitro differentiation assays (using primary osteoblasts and chondrocytes treated with inhibitors at 10 nM–1 µM concentrations), and in vivo mouse models of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), osteoarthritis, and osteoporosis (with dosing regimens of 5–20 mg/kg administered intravenously). Key outcomes will include enhanced bone density (measured by µCT), cartilage thickness (assessed via histology), and reduced ectopic bone formation (quantified by micro-radiography), demonstrating the therapeutic potential of this dual-targeted strategy in restoring skeletal homeostasis and treating bone and cartilage disorders. This approach addresses the limitations of current therapies, such as non-specificity and off-target effects, and has broader applications in diseases involving BMP-TGF-β signaling dysregulation, including cancer and fibrosis.
